2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Reagents and antibodies
Antibodies used for flow cytometry included PE‐CD34, PE-CD235a (GPA), and APC‐α4 integrin (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany); PE‐Cy7‐Annexin V (eBioscience, San Diego, California); and human band 3, which was generated in our laboratory and labeled with FITC. Dyes used for flow cytometry were PerCP‐Cy5.5‐7AAD, propidium iodide (BD Pharmingen, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey), and Hoechst 33342 (BD Pharmingen). All flow cytometry experiments were performed in triplicate.
2.2. Cell culture and fluorescence-activated cell sorting
Human umbilical cord blood samples were obtained from Xiangya Hospital of Central South University with approval from the institutional ethics committee. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. The isolated CD34
+
cells and sorted cell populations were cultured as previously described.
10
2.3. LC/LC-MS/MS for proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis
The sorted cell samples were subjected to protein extraction, trypsin digestion, and TMT labeling as previously described.
10
For proteomic analysis, peptide mixtures were incubated for 2 hours at room temperature, pooled, desalted, and dried by vacuum centrifugation, followed by HPLC fractionation using an Agilent 300Extend C18 column (Thermo Scientific, Shanghai, China). For phosphoproteomic analysis, peptides were sequentially fractionated using a Thermo Betasil C18 column with biomaterial-based phosphorylation enrichment. The resulting phosphopeptide-containing supernatant was collected and lyophilized for LC-MS/MS analysis using a Thermo Scientific Q Exactive HF-X Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with an H-ESI II ion source and an EASY-nLC 1200 UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific, Shanghai, China), as previously described.
10
Tandem mass spectral data were acquired as described previously.
10
2.4. Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses for each plot were described in the relevant sections or figure legends. All grouped data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation.
p
Values were calculated using either Student
t
test or Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA in GraphPad Prism software.
2.5. Data availability
The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium (
http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org
) via the iProX partner repository under the dataset identifier PXD035785.75.

1. INTRODUCTION
Erythropoiesis, a major branch of hematopoiesis, is responsible for producing specialized red blood cells (RBCs) that play a vital role in systemic oxygen transport.
1
A defining feature of mammalian terminal erythropoiesis is the expulsion of the highly condensed nucleus from the cytoplasm during the final stage of differentiation.
2
This process, termed enucleation, not only creates additional cytoplasmic space for hemoglobin synthesis but also provides RBCs with the flexibility required to traverse narrow capillaries.
3
Following enucleation, reticulocytes undergo further maturation through sequential membrane remodeling, proteomic reprogramming, and organelle clearance.
2
,
3
Accumulating evidence indicates that protein phosphorylation and associated regulatory networks are critical for orchestrating erythrocyte enucleation and reticulocyte maturation.
4
For example, phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) regulates vesicle biogenesis,
5
phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-mediated signaling controls cell polarization,
6
E2F transcription factor 2/citron Rho-interacting kinase (E2F-2/CRIK) modulates nuclear condensation,
7
and Ulk1 drives autophagy-dependent mitochondrial clearance.
8
,
9
Despite these advances, the dynamic landscape of protein phosphorylation during erythroblast enucleation and subsequent reticulocyte maturation—key processes in late-terminal erythroid differentiation—remains poorly characterized.
In this study, we systematically profiled the proteome and phosphoproteome of umbilical cord blood (UBC)-derived erythroblasts (at the enucleation stage), reticulocytes, and mature RBCs. To achieve this, we combined tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling with 2-dimensional liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC/LC-MS/MS). Integrated with bioinformatics analyses, our findings provide a comprehensive overview of dynamic protein phosphorylation events and the core signaling pathways that regulate erythroid enucleation and maturation. Collectively, these results reveal the dynamic signaling networks and selective bioenergetic pathways that underlie nuclear remodeling and cellular survival during erythrocyte maturation.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Reagents and antibodies
Antibodies used for flow cytometry included PE‐CD34, PE-CD235a (GPA), and APC‐α4 integrin (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany); PE‐Cy7‐Annexin V (eBioscience, San Diego, California); and human band 3, which was generated in our laboratory and labeled with FITC. Dyes used for flow cytometry were PerCP‐Cy5.5‐7AAD, propidium iodide (BD Pharmingen, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey), and Hoechst 33342 (BD Pharmingen). All flow cytometry experiments were performed in triplicate.
2.2. Cell culture and fluorescence-activated cell sorting
Human umbilical cord blood samples were obtained from Xiangya Hospital of Central South University with approval from the institutional ethics committee. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. The isolated CD34
+
cells and sorted cell populations were cultured as previously described.
10
2.3. LC/LC-MS/MS for proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis
The sorted cell samples were subjected to protein extraction, trypsin digestion, and TMT labeling as previously described.
10
For proteomic analysis, peptide mixtures were incubated for 2 hours at room temperature, pooled, desalted, and dried by vacuum centrifugation, followed by HPLC fractionation using an Agilent 300Extend C18 column (Thermo Scientific, Shanghai, China). For phosphoproteomic analysis, peptides were sequentially fractionated using a Thermo Betasil C18 column with biomaterial-based phosphorylation enrichment. The resulting phosphopeptide-containing supernatant was collected and lyophilized for LC-MS/MS analysis using a Thermo Scientific Q Exactive HF-X Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with an H-ESI II ion source and an EASY-nLC 1200 UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific, Shanghai, China), as previously described.
10
Tandem mass spectral data were acquired as described previously.
10
2.4. Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses for each plot were described in the relevant sections or figure legends. All grouped data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation.
p
Values were calculated using either Student
t
test or Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA in GraphPad Prism software.
2.5. Data availability
The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium (
http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org
) via the iProX partner repository under the dataset identifier PXD035785.75.
11
3. RESULTS
3.1. Establishing the whole proteome and phosphoproteome profiling of human erythroid enucleation and maturation
After 17 days of culture in the erythropoietin (EPO)-induced CD34
+
erythroid differentiation system, cells were collected, stained with Hoechst 33342, and sorted using a Beckman MoFlo Astrios flow cytometer and its associated software (Fig.
1
A). Hoechst 33342 staining effectively separated the cells into Hoechst-positive and Hoechst-negative populations. Flow cytometric analysis confirmed that the purity of the sorted cells, including UBC-derived mature RBCs, was ≥95% (Fig.
1
B). May–Grünwald–Giemsa staining revealed that preenucleation erythroblasts (Eblasts) were predominantly orthochromatic erythroblasts (Ortho-E), whereas postenucleation cells were reticulocytes (Retics) (Fig.
1
C).
Figure 1.
Establishing the whole proteome and phosphoproteome profiling of human erythroid enucleation and maturation. A, Schematic workflow. B, Purity analysis of sorted cells by flow cytometry. C, Morphology and purity of sorted cells observed by MGG staining (scale bar = 20 μm). D, The subcellular distribution of proteins across all cell populations based on subcellular annotations from the Human Protein Atlas. E, Distribution of different residue types (pS/pT/pY) of phosphorylation sites during erythrocyte enucleation, where pS represents phosphorylated serine residues, pT phosphorylated threonine residues, and pY phosphorylated tyrosine residues. F, Subcellular distribution of proteins corresponding to phosphorylated peptides in all cell populations annotated based on the Human Protein Atlas. G, Hierarchical clustering analysis of protein expression abundance at different stages of erythroid enucleation and maturation. H, Hierarchical clustering analysis of modification levels of proteins corresponding to phosphorylated peptides at erythroid enucleation and maturation stages, showing 5 co-expression clusters with color representing protein detection abundance. I and J, GO enrichment analysis (FDR < 0.05) of proteins (I) and corresponding to phosphorylated peptides (J) expression clusters show in (G) and (H). CB-RBCs = cord blood-derived mature red blood cells, FDR = false discovery rate, GO = Gene Ontology, LC/LC-MS/MS = liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry, MGG = May–Grünwald–Giemsa, TMT = tandem mass tag.
Proteomic analysis was performed using TMT labeling combined with LC-MS/MS, yielding 349,067 secondary spectra, of which 15,018 (4.3%) were valid for quantification. Quantitative analysis revealed a comparable number of proteins across the stages of erythroid enucleation and maturation, with 1641, 1632, and 1627 quantifiable proteins identified in Eblasts, Retics, and RBCs, respectively. Subcellular localization analysis, based on the Human Protein Atlas, showed a clear shift from nuclear to cytoplasmic localization during erythroid maturation (Fig.
1
D). Unlike the early erythroid stage, which is dominated by nuclear proteins, only 406 proteins (24.7% of the total) were localized in the nucleus during enucleation and maturation. The majority were located in the cytoplasm and organelles, consistent with nuclear pyknosis, condensation, and expulsion, which characterize erythrocyte maturation.
Similarly, phosphoproteomic analysis using TMT labeling and phosphorylation enrichment followed by LC-MS/MS generated 32,185 spectra, of which 1874 (5.82%) were valid for analysis. Quantitative profiling identified 619 and 573 phosphorylated peptides in the pre- and postenucleation stages (Eblasts and Retics), and 573 in mature RBCs. Analysis of phosphorylation sites revealed that serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues accounted for 89.18%, 9.37%, and 1.45% of all sites, respectively (Fig.
1
E). Subcellular localization of the 398 phosphorylated proteins revealed that 41.21% (164 proteins) were nuclear, whereas 28.64% (114 proteins) were cytoplasmic, suggesting a potential regulatory role for phosphorylation in nuclear expulsion during erythropoiesis (Fig.
1
F).
To further investigate the temporal dynamics of protein expression and phosphorylation during erythroid enucleation and maturation, hierarchical clustering analysis was conducted. This analysis revealed 6 distinct co-expression clusters based on protein expression patterns (Fig.
1
G). Specifically, clusters 1 and 5 exhibited high expression at the reticulocyte stage, clusters 2 and 3 displayed progressive downregulation, cluster 4 showed reduced expression at the reticulocyte stage, and cluster 6 demonstrated gradual upregulation throughout the process. Similarly, hierarchical clustering of phosphorylated proteins based on their phosphorylation levels identified 5 distinct clusters (Fig.
1
H). Cluster 1 exhibited a gradual increase in phosphorylation, cluster 2 showed low phosphorylation at the reticulocyte stage, cluster 3 showed high phosphorylation at the reticulocyte stage, cluster 4 displayed elevated phosphorylation in nucleated erythroblasts, and cluster 5 showed low phosphorylation in mature RBCs. These findings underscore the stage-specific phosphorylation patterns that likely regulate key events during erythroid differentiation.
We next performed Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the proteins in each expression cluster (Fig.
1
I). Cluster 1 was enriched in processes related to protein and RNA localization and translational initiation; cluster 2 was associated with energy metabolism, proton transport, and mitochondrial organization; cluster 3 with RNA splicing, actin organization, and phagocytosis; cluster 4 with U2 snRNP, protein folding, vacuolar lumen, lipid droplets, and melanosome-related processes; cluster 5 with metabolic processes and protein neddylation regulation; and cluster 6 with detoxification, oxygen transport, hydrogen peroxide metabolism, and regulation of actin depolymerization (Fig.
1
I). Similarly, GO analysis of phosphorylated protein clusters (Fig.
1
J) showed that cluster 1 was associated with actin capping, CO₂ transport, protein binding regulation, and oxidant detoxification; cluster 2 with cell polarity, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) signaling, and K63-linked ubiquitination; cluster 3 with osmotic stress response, proteolysis regulation, and branched polyubiquitination; cluster 4 with RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein biogenesis, and microtubule organization; and cluster 5 with complex disassembly, deubiquitination, and negative regulation of proteasomal degradation (Fig.
1
J).
3.2. Differential analysis of the whole proteome and phosphoproteome across stages of human erythroid enucleation and maturation
We conducted differential expression analysis between samples using generalized fold change (GFOLD) software (Fig.
2
A and B). During erythrocyte enucleation (Eblasts vs Retics), 180 molecules were upregulated, including members of the keratin family (KRT1, KRT2, etc), LGALS, APOE, and MYL4, whereas 366 molecules, including histone H2AFX and the vesicle transport factor USO1, were downregulated (Fig.
2
A). During the reticulocyte maturation stage (Retics vs RBCs), 168 proteins, including SRXN1 and BLOC1S5, were upregulated, whereas 256 proteins, such as keratin family members and APOE, were downregulated (Fig.
2
B). Phosphoproteomic analysis revealed 186 upregulated and 189 downregulated phosphorylation sites during erythrocyte enucleation (Fig.
2
C). During reticulocyte maturation, 130 phosphorylation sites were upregulated and 164 were downregulated (Fig.
2
D).
Figure 2.
Differential analysis of the whole proteome and phosphoproteome across stages of human erythroid enucleation and maturation. A and B, Scatter plots of protein abundance between 2 adjacent erythroid differentiation stages, where the color of each point represents the magnitude of the GFOLD value. C and D, Scatter plots depicting changes in phosphorylated protein abundance between 2 adjacent erythroid differentiation stages, where point color indicates the magnitude of GFOLD values. E and F, GO enrichment results for differentially phosphorylated proteins in the comparison of Ebasts vs Retics (E) or Retics vs RBCs (F). G, Flow cytometric detection of GPA-positive rate in erythroid differentiated cells stained with PE-CD235a after treatment with different apoptosis inducers, with the percentage in red font indicating the GPA-positive rate. H, Flow cytometric detection of enucleation rate of in vitro induced erythroid differentiated cells treated with different apoptosis inducers, which were stained with Hoechst 33342, and enucleated cells were Hoechst 33342-negative. Statistics are shown as the mean ± SD. Comparisons between 2 groups were evaluated with a 2-tailed
t
test, and comparisons among multiple groups were evaluated with one-way ANOVA. *
p
< 0.050; **
p
< 0.010; ***
p
< .001. DMSO = dimethyl sulfoxide, GFOLD = generalized fold change, RBC = red blood cell.
Subsequently, GO enrichment analysis of differentially phosphorylated proteins (Fig.
2
E and F) indicated that proteins involved in enucleation were enriched in biological processes such as cellular response to osmotic stress, positive regulation of the intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway, RNA splicing, and translational initiation (Fig.
2
E). During reticulocyte maturation, differentially phosphorylated proteins were enriched in pathways related to carbon dioxide transport, hydrogen peroxide catabolism, and acetyl-CoA metabolism (Fig.
2
F). These findings suggest that apoptosis plays a crucial role in erythrocyte enucleation. To validate this observation, terminally differentiated erythroid cells were treated with two apoptosis inducers, etoposide
12
and cisplatin.
13
Both compounds significantly reduced the proportion of GPA (CD235a)-positive erythroid cells in culture (Fig.
2
G) and markedly decreased the enucleation rate of terminally differentiated erythroblasts (Fig.
2
H).
4. DISCUSSION
Limited stem cell sources, high costs, poor expansion, and low enucleation efficiency continue to hinder in vitro RBC production.
14
Additionally, in vitro-derived reticulocytes exhibit reduced survival times, restricting their application in clinical transfusion and biomaterial development. In this study, we systematically characterized dynamic alterations in protein expression and phosphorylation through comprehensive proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses during erythroid enucleation and maturation. We further investigated the involvement of apoptosis-related pathways in enucleation, providing insights into the regulatory roles of kinases and other associated proteins in this process.
Notably, the cellular response to osmotic stress emerged as the most enriched biological term during enucleation, consistent with previous findings indicating that osmotic stress influences chromatin condensation and nucleocytoplasmic transport,
15
working synergistically with histone deacetylase-mediated remodeling and actomyosin dynamics to promote nuclear extrusion.
16
Consequently, manipulating osmotic pressure may represent a viable strategy to enhance in vitro RBC production.
To better delineate proteomic dynamics during erythroid development, Gautier et al
17
employed label-free quantitative mass spectrometry to profile the proteome across all erythroid differentiation stages. They also used iTRAQ-based quantitative proteomics to compare protein distribution between in vitro-generated reticulocytes and nucleated erythroid cells, identifying proteins associated with enucleation.
17
Chu et al
18
applied CD71-based separation and iTRAQ mass spectrometry to identify >1800 proteins in UBC–derived reticulocytes and mature RBCs. Moura et al
4
integrated microfiltration with phosphoproteomics to examine erythrocyte membrane deformation, highlighting the critical roles for GSK3 and Lyn in maintaining membrane stability under mechanical stress. Inhibition of these kinases impairs reticulocyte deformability. Collectively, this phosphoproteomics dataset, together with our analysis of enucleation-related phosphorylation events, provides valuable resources for investigating the molecular mechanisms governing RBC responses to mechanical stimuli and reticulocyte maturation.
Accumulating evidence indicates that unresolved DNA damage can trigger genomic instability, apoptosis, or senescence, thereby influencing both development and aging. Furthermore, the loss of genomic integrity may result in immune deficiencies, neurological disorders, and cancer.
19
Defective DNA repair mechanisms in HSCs have been linked to bone marrow failure and leukemia progression.
20
,
21
Because DNA synthesis, damage, repair, and apoptosis occur concurrently during erythroid progenitor development, these cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress. Peroxisome II plays a protective role in maintaining DNA integrity and supporting normal erythropoiesis.
22
EPO also promotes erythroid survival by reducing DNA damage and preventing apoptosis, thus enabling the progenitors to proceed with terminal differentiation.
23
DNA damage repair is closely associated with reticulocyte formation and maturation. In 1997, Koury et al
24
demonstrated that DNA damage correlated with apoptosis in late erythroid precursors in a megaloblastic anemia model. The study further revealed that reduced thymidine synthesis was a principal cause of apoptosis in folate-deficient erythroid precursor cells.
25
Although extensive research has addressed early erythropoiesis, the function of DNA integrity in late-stage processes, particularly enucleation, remains inadequately understood and merits further exploration. Our findings suggest that apoptotic pathways also contribute significantly to erythroid enucleation; however, the precise mechanisms require further elucidation.
5. CONCLUSIONS
This study provides foundational data and a theoretical framework for elucidating the mechanisms underlying erythrocyte enucleation and enhancing the enucleation efficiency of in vitro–cultured erythrocytes. These findings suggest that regulating osmotic stress, kinase activity, and DNA damage responses may improve both the efficiency and quality of in vitro RBC production.
